entries.test: Company financial disclosures and reporting on AI investment, profitability, and released product capabilities would test the factual claims about spending and commercial results as of publication.
entries.note: The usefulness language is evaluative and hedged, but the spending and profitability assertions are factual.
The central claim attributes a private motive to Google's decision.

entries.test: Google's actual replacement of Assistant with Gemini, together with public evidence of Gemini's capabilities and hallucinations at replacement, would test the forecast.
entries.note: In context, 'the writing is on the wall' expresses a firm expectation. No deadline is specified.
The integration plans are independently checkable, but the complete claim attributes private motives to both companies.

entries.test: Public land acquisition records, company capital expenditure disclosures, and reporting on AI data center projects would establish the acreage and spending as of publication.
entries.note: The claim has concrete numerical commitments, although whether the spending has a 'compelling reason' is evaluative.
The contrast between economies and assertion that the industry has 'run out of ideas' constitute polemical exaggeration rather than a defined causal test.

entries.test: Published operating costs, documented errors, and independent tests of problems that vendors promoted generative AI as solving would test the claim as of publication.
entries.note: The unspecified problems broaden the evidence needed but leave a plain factual reading about promoted capabilities exceeding demonstrated capabilities.

entries.test: Microsoft's Super Bowl advertisement and reproducible tests of the advertised Copilot tasks using the contemporaneous product would show whether the depicted results misrepresented its capabilities.
entries.note: The 'compelling description' language is subjective, but the allegation that the advertisement misrepresented product results has a concrete public test.
